cls: Polyphenolic stilbene phytoalexin - dietary supplement / antioxidant
quick: Supplement: commonly 150-500 mg PO once daily (no approved therapeutic dose)
Often taken with food; absorption is low regardless of meal
Avoid - insufficient safety data; not recommended in pregnancy
Avoid - insufficient safety data during breastfeeding
No established dose adjustment; caution, limited data
Caution at high doses; high-dose supplements reported to raise liver enzymes
Found naturally in red wine but supplement use does not justify alcohol intake
Not routinely required; consider LFTs and bleeding risk at high doses
summary: Resveratrol is a naturally occurring polyphenolic stilbene found in grape skins, red wine, peanuts and certain berries, marketed as a dietary supplement for purported antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, cardiovascular and metabolic benefits. It is NOT an FDA-approved drug and has no approved therapeutic indication; evidence for clinical benefit is preliminary and inconsistent. Oral bioavailability is very low because of extensive first-pass glucuronidation and sulfation. It is generally well tolerated at supplement doses, with GI upset and possible antiplatelet/CYP-modulating effects at high doses. This record is based on supplement monographs and the published literature rather than an FDA label.
indications: No approved therapeutic indication - marketed as a dietary supplement
Investigational/supplement use for cardiovascular health, metabolic support and antioxidant effect (efficacy not established)

dosage.d: Commonly 150-500 mg PO once daily as a supplement
dosage.n: No standardised or approved dose; products vary widely in purity and content

dosage.d: Up to 1000-2000 mg/day used in some clinical studies
dosage.n: Higher doses associated with more GI side effects; not an endorsement of efficacy

admin: Take orally as capsules/tablets, typically with food to reduce GI upset
Be aware oral bioavailability is very low due to rapid metabolism
Choose products from reputable manufacturers - supplement quality is not FDA-regulated as for drugs
Separate from other supplements/medications if GI intolerance occurs
Discontinue before surgery because of possible antiplatelet effect
moa: Resveratrol is a polyphenolic antioxidant that scavenges free radicals and modulates several signalling pathways. Proposed mechanisms include activation of sirtuin (SIRT1) and AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) pathways, inhibition of cyclooxygenase and platelet aggregation, and modulation of estrogen receptors (phytoestrogen activity). These actions are largely derived from laboratory and animal studies, and clinical relevance in humans is not established.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to resveratrol or product excipients
relative: Hormone-sensitive conditions (breast, uterine, ovarian cancer; endometriosis; uterine fibroids) due to estrogenic activity
Bleeding disorders or use of anticoagulants/antiplatelets
Upcoming surgery (stop at least 2 weeks before)

preg: There are insufficient safety data in pregnancy and resveratrol has estrogenic activity. It is not recommended during pregnancy; avoid supplemental use.
lact: Safety during breastfeeding has not been established and there are no adequate human data. Avoid supplemental resveratrol while breastfeeding.
renal: No established dose adjustment in renal impairment; data are limited. Use cautiously and avoid very high doses.
hepatic: Resveratrol is extensively metabolised in the liver and gut. High-dose supplementation has been associated with elevations of liver enzymes in some reports; use caution in hepatic impairment and monitor if high doses are taken.

major: Anticoagulants/antiplatelets (warfarin, aspirin, clopidogrel) - possible additive bleeding risk
moderate: Substrates of CYP3A4, CYP2C9, CYP1A2 - resveratrol can inhibit these enzymes and raise levels of affected drugs
Other agents metabolised by UGT/sulfotransferases (competition for conjugation)
minor: Iron and certain minerals (polyphenols may reduce absorption)
interactions.food: Naturally present in red wine, grapes and peanuts; taking with food may lessen GI upset but does not improve the low bioavailability much
interactions.alcohol: Although found in red wine, do not use supplements as a reason to consume alcohol; no protective interaction is established
interactions.diagnostics: May affect platelet function tests; no specific assay interference established

serious: Increased bleeding risk when combined with anticoagulants/antiplatelets
Liver enzyme elevation at high doses
rare: Possible hormone-sensitive tissue stimulation due to estrogenic activity
Renal effects with very high prolonged dosing (limited reports)

monitoring: Not routinely required at usual supplement doses
Liver function tests if high doses are used long term
Signs of bleeding/bruising in patients on antithrombotic therapy
Symptoms in patients with hormone-sensitive conditions
counsel: This is a dietary supplement, not an approved medicine; benefits are not proven
Tell your doctor you take it, especially if you use blood thinners or are scheduled for surgery
Stop at least two weeks before any planned operation
Buy from reputable brands since supplement content and purity are not tightly regulated
pk: Not defined for a therapeutic effect
Plasma peak approximately 0.5-1.5 hours; oral bioavailability very low (<1% as parent)
Parent resveratrol approximately 1-3 hours; conjugated metabolites circulate longer (about 9-11 hours)
Short systemic exposure due to rapid metabolism
Store at room temperature in a cool, dry place away from light; keep tightly closed
pearls: Resveratrol is NOT FDA-approved as a drug - it is a dietary supplement; clinical efficacy claims are unproven and product quality is variable (this record is based on supplement monographs/literature, not an FDA label)
Very low oral bioavailability (extensive first-pass glucuronidation/sulfation) limits achievable plasma levels of the parent compound
Can inhibit CYP3A4/2C9 and platelet function - review for interactions with anticoagulants and narrow-therapeutic-index drugs
Has phytoestrogen activity; avoid in hormone-sensitive cancers and during pregnancy
Stop before surgery because of a theoretical bleeding risk
missed: As a supplement there is no strict schedule; if you miss a dose simply take the next one as usual. Do not double up. Consistency matters more than catching up on a missed dose.
overdose: Acute toxicity appears low; very high doses mainly cause gastrointestinal upset (nausea, diarrhea, cramping). There is no specific antidote - treat supportively with hydration and symptom control, and discontinue the supplement.
